newsitem.title: USA: Intel to continue Pentium supplies to Digital.
newsitem.headline: Intel to continue Pentium supplies to Digital.

text.p: Intel Corp., which threatened to stop shipping Pentium chips to Digital Equipment Corp. in a battle over copyrights last spring, has agreed to continue shipping them through year-end, Digital said Wednesday.
Digital also alleged in court papers filed in a federal court in California that Intel has wielded "monopoly power" to harm Digital for selling a competing computer chip.

"We recently got a commitment from Intel for Q4 (fourth quarter) supply," Digital spokesman Dan Kaferle told Reuters. "They are going to supply us chips. We'll continue to develop Intel-based systems on par with market requirements."
Kaferle did not comment on the size of the fourth-quarter shipments. Intel spokesman Chuck Mulloy declined to comment on its supply agreement with Digital.

In May, after Digital sued the chip manufacturer for allegedly stealing key semiconductor secrets and infringing on a handful of patents, Intel retaliated by threatening to cut off the supply of Pentium chips. Intel also sued Digital, demanding the return of documents about the design of Merced, Intel's next generation of microprocessers.
In 1996, Digital sold $2.2 billion worth of computers that use Intel chips, more than a quarter of its product revenues of $8.4 billion.

In letters sent to Digital executives in May, Intel said Digital's current purchase order runs out in the third quarter. Digital, based in Maynard, Mass., said its product agreement with Intel ran through 1999 and it did not expect any interruptions.
Santa Clara, Calif.-based Intel has denied the allegations of patent infringement. Lawyers have said that any move by Intel to cut off supply could raise antitrust issues.

In court papers filed in federal court in San Jose, Calif., Digital said Intel had a market share "approaching 90 percent" in the domestic and global market for microprocessors, and was trying to "retain that market share and the power that market share gives it."
Digital also alleged that Intel is "acting in bad faith and in violation of antitrust law" by demanding the return of Merced documents.
Intel's Mulloy said the court papers contained "just the kind of language that they have used in public statements and press releases since the beginning of the litigation."
Digital said Monday it agreed to return the documents, which were more than a year old, and had no plans on helping the chip company develop the Merced microprocessor.

Analysts have said that Digital could be at a huge disadvantage to competitors such as International Business Machines Corp., Compaq Computer Corp. and others if it were denied access to Intel's plans.
